144	## 4. Derivation Chains
145	
146	Show how the ground truths combine into conclusions. Every conclusion offered in this analysis must have exactly one chain here — no more (no redundant restatement), no fewer (no orphaned conclusions).
147	
148	**Chain numbering convention.** Number each `### Conclusion:` block in this section `C1`,
149	`C2`, ... in document order (e.g., `### Conclusion C1: [Conclusion text]`). The §6→§4
150	closure ledger (the agent body — `SKILL.md` on the skill surface, `agents/first-principles.md` on the agent surface — "Before presenting conclusions") cites these IDs when mapping a
151	Conclusion-section (section 6) claim back to the chain in this section that established it.
152	
153	**Chain format:**
154	
155	```text
156	GT-N + GT-M → [intermediate claim] → [conclusion]
157	```
158	
159	The one-line form is the degenerate case, used only when the whole chain fits on one physical line; a chain that does not fit uses the head-plus-arrow-led form, and a hop is split rather than continued on a second line.
160	
161	Each chain must contain at least one intermediate step. A chain that goes directly from its head inputs to conclusion is incomplete — the intermediate is where the reasoning happens. The intermediate must be a new claim that could not be stated from any single head input alone. If no intermediate can be stated, the conclusion is either a restatement of a head input (trivial) or a reasoning step is missing.
162	
163	**No-wrap rule.** A hop occupies exactly one physical line. Every line after the head begins with `→` and carries exactly one complete hop; a hop is never broken across physical lines. A chain needing more hops continues on further arrow-led lines. A hop too long for comfort is SPLIT, not wrapped — the analysis renders as Markdown, so a long hop soft-wraps for the reader without breaking the form.
164	
165	```text
166	GT-1 ([brief fact label]) + GT-6 ([brief fact label])
167	→ [intermediate claim]
168	→ [further intermediate]
169	→ [conclusion]
170	```
171	
172	**Head-input rule.** The head line lists the inputs the chain consumes: each is a `GT-N` identifier (`GT-N?` when the ground truth is unverified) or a `Cn` identifier, optionally followed by a parenthesized gloss, joined to the next by `+`. The first `→` closes the head. An input carrying unparenthesized prose — `C2's threshold` — is not an identifier and does not parse; write `C2 (threshold)` in every position. The mechanical form check detects that violation only when the prose input is the last one before the first `→`; in an earlier position the check matches the well-formed remainder and scores the head conforming, so the rule binds in positions the check does not reach.
173	
174	```text
175	GT-1? ([brief fact label]) + C2 ([brief fact label])
176	→ [intermediate claim]
177	→ [conclusion]
178	```
179	
180	The head grammar governs the head line only. A hop is prose: `C2's saving` is fine after the first `→`, and is not an input reference. One exception: a hop must not begin with a `GT-N` identifier, which the form check reads as the head of a new chain and which therefore ends this one — write `→ the duty cycle stated in GT-4 is the binding term`, not `→ GT-4's stated duty cycle is the binding term`. The form check detects that violation only while fewer than two hops precede it; in a later position the check matches the preceding hops and scores the chain conforming, so the rule binds in positions the check does not reach.
181	
182	The mechanical form check additionally rejects a chain whose head or first hop closes its own sentence before the next `→`: it reads the following arrow-led line as a new statement and ends the chain there, so a chain satisfying every rule above is scored malformed for that reason alone. The check reaches only that position — a hop that closes its own sentence from the second hop onward does not change the verdict — which is why intermediate hops carry no terminal punctuation in this project's worked examples.
183	
184	**Conforming — head, then one hop per line:**
185	
186	```text
187	GT-1 (Lambda $/GB-s, AWS pricing) + GT-6 (Fargate $/vCPU-hr, AWS pricing)
188	→ Lambda costs 2.10× per unit of actual compute
189	→ sustained workloads belong on Fargate
190	```
191	
192	**Non-conforming — a hop broken across physical lines:**
193	
194	```text
195	GT-1 (Lambda $/GB-s, AWS pricing) + GT-6 (Fargate $/vCPU-hr, AWS pricing)
196	→ Lambda costs 2.10× per unit of actual compute
197	  once idle-time billing is included
198	→ sustained workloads belong on Fargate
199	```
200	
201	The continuation line does not begin with `→`, so the chain terminates at the head's first hop and what remains reads as an incomplete chain.
202	
203	**Non-conforming — the same hops rendered as a numbered list:**
204	
205	```text
206	1. GT-1 (Lambda $/GB-s, AWS pricing) + GT-6 (Fargate $/vCPU-hr, AWS pricing)
207	2. Lambda costs 2.10× per unit of actual compute
208	3. sustained workloads belong on Fargate
209	```
210	
211	A numbered list restates each hop as its own GT-headed one-hop chain, which reads as several incomplete chains rather than one complete one — the intermediate steps stop being connected to the conclusion they build toward.
212	
213	**Non-conforming — an input carrying unparenthesized prose:**
214	
215	```text
216	GT-13? (bill composition unknown) + GT-12? (duty cycle unknown) + C2's threshold
217	→ target quantity: fraction of total AWS bill removed by the migration
218	→ the bracket straddles zero, so its two ends recommend opposite actions
219	```
220	
221	`C2's threshold` is not an identifier — it is a possessive prose phrase — so the head does not parse; the third input must be written `C2 (threshold)`.
222	
223	**Conforming — the same head with the upstream chain as an input:**
224	
225	```text
226	GT-13? (bill composition unknown) + GT-12? (duty cycle unknown) + C2 (threshold)
227	→ target quantity: fraction of total AWS bill removed by the migration
228	→ the bracket straddles zero, so its two ends recommend opposite actions
229	```
230	
231	Exactly one token differs from the block above: a `Cn` identifier with a parenthesized gloss is an admissible head input, on equal footing with a `GT-N` identifier.
232	
233	**Conforming — a chain consuming only upstream conclusions:**
234	
235	```text
236	C1 (2.20× at full duty) + C2 (conditional on an unmeasured threshold) + C4 (unconditional, zero code change) + C5 (~73% ceiling, no execution-model change)
237	→ C4 and C5 deliver verified savings that do not depend on any property of your workload
238	→ C2's saving depends entirely on a duty-cycle figure nobody has measured
239	```
240	
241	A head may consist entirely of `Cn` inputs with no `GT-N` term. The second hop's `C2's saving` is prose, not a head input — the head-only scope note is what permits it here.
242	
243	**Non-conforming, and undetected by the form check — the same prose input in a non-final position:**
244	
245	```text
246	GT-13? (bill composition unknown) + C2's threshold + GT-12? (duty cycle unknown)
247	→ target quantity: fraction of total AWS bill removed by the migration
248	→ the bracket straddles zero, so its two ends recommend opposite actions
249	```
250	
251	This head breaks the same rule as the non-conforming block above and is equally non-conforming, but the mechanical form check scores it conforming — with a well-formed input still to its right the check matches from `GT-12?` onward and never reaches `C2's threshold`. Write `C2 (threshold)` wherever the input sits; the rule is the contract, and the check is a partial instrument for it.
252	
253	**Non-conforming — a hop beginning with a GT-N identifier:**
254	
255	```text
256	C1 (2.20× at full duty) + C2 (conditional on an unmeasured threshold)
257	→ GT-4's stated duty cycle is the binding term in both estimates
258	→ the bracket straddles zero, so its two ends recommend opposite actions
259	```
260	
261	The second line reads as the head of a new chain because it begins with a `GT-N` identifier, so this chain ends after its head and what remains is an incomplete chain — the possessive is not the problem, the leading identifier is.
262	
263	**Conforming — the same hop with the identifier moved off the front:**
264	
265	```text
266	C1 (2.20× at full duty) + C2 (conditional on an unmeasured threshold)
267	→ the duty cycle stated in GT-4 is the binding term in both estimates
268	→ the bracket straddles zero, so its two ends recommend opposite actions
269	```
270	
271	Exactly one clause is reordered and the chain is whole again; naming a ground truth inside a hop is fine, leading with its identifier is not.
272	
273	**Non-conforming, and undetected by the form check — the GT-led hop in a later position:**
274	
275	```text
276	C1 (2.20× at full duty) + C2 (conditional on an unmeasured threshold)
277	→ the bracket straddles zero, so its two ends recommend opposite actions
278	→ the second reading is the binding one
279	→ GT-4's stated duty cycle is the binding term in both estimates
280	```
281	
282	This hop breaks the same rule as the non-conforming block above and is equally non-conforming, but the mechanical form check scores it conforming — the check has already satisfied its two-arrow requirement on the hops that precede it, so the leading identifier ends the chain there without changing the verdict. Write `→ the duty cycle stated in GT-4 is the binding term in both estimates` wherever the hop sits; the rule is the contract, and the check is a partial instrument for it.
283	
284	**Non-conforming — the first hop closing its own sentence:**
285	
286	```text
287	C1 (2.20× at full duty) + C2 (conditional on an unmeasured threshold)
288	→ C1's saving is unconditional and does not depend on workload shape.
289	→ C2's saving is real only above the duty-cycle threshold this estimate assumes
290	```
291	
292	This chain violates none of R1-R9 — every input parses, every hop states one inference, no hop leads with a `GT-N` identifier — and is scored malformed anyway, because the mechanical form check ends the chain the moment the first hop closes its own sentence, before its two-arrow requirement is satisfied, and never reaches the well-formed hop that follows.
293	
294	**Conforming — the same chain with the first hop's terminal period removed:**
295	
296	```text
297	C1 (2.20× at full duty) + C2 (conditional on an unmeasured threshold)
298	→ C1's saving is unconditional and does not depend on workload shape
299	→ C2's saving is real only above the duty-cycle threshold this estimate assumes
300	```
301	
302	Exactly one character differs from the block above: the terminal period. Removing it, and nothing else, restores the two-arrow match the check requires.
303	
304	**Non-conforming, and undetected by the form check — the same period moved to a later hop:**
305	
306	```text
307	C1 (2.20× at full duty) + C2 (conditional on an unmeasured threshold)
308	→ C1's saving is unconditional and does not depend on workload shape
309	→ the migration case does not rest on C1 alone
310	→ C2's saving is real only above the duty-cycle threshold this estimate assumes.
311	```
312	
313	This block breaks the identical rule one hop later and is equally non-conforming, but the mechanical form check scores it conforming — with two hops already matched before the closing sentence is reached, the check has satisfied its two-arrow requirement and the sentence-closing period on the third hop has no following line left to block. Write the closing hop with no terminal punctuation wherever it sits; the rule is the contract, and the check is a partial instrument for it.
314	
315	**One-inference rule.** A hop states exactly ONE inference. If a hop joins two claims with "and", or carries a parenthetical that could stand as its own claim, it is two hops — split it.
316	
317	TELL (not the rule): a hop past ~200 characters is almost always two hops. Measure the hop, then split — do not wrap it, and do not trim words to hit a number.
318	
319	Inline annotations (`*[Assumes: A14 — …]*`) attach to the end of the hop line they qualify and do not start a new hop.
320	
321	### Converting structured-technique outputs into chains
322	
323	Structured-technique outputs (trade-off matrices, second-order effect lists) do not appear in this section as-is — each converts into the chain format above using the rule for its technique below. This subsection is the single source of truth for the conversion; the per-technique Handoff sections point back here rather than restating it, so future structured techniques extend this one place.
324	
325	**Trade-off matrix → one chain.** A trade-off matrix collapses into ONE chain whose intermediate cites the winning weighted total and whose endpoint names a single recommended option:
326	
327	```text
328	GT-refs (criteria's factual basis) → weighted totals (the winning total vs. the runner-up, naming the high-weight criteria that drive it) → recommended option
329	```
330	
331	Example: `GT-2 + GT-5 (criteria facts) → weighted totals: B=82 > A=64, driven by reliability×warranty → recommend B`. The full matrix stays in the technique's own output — this subsection carries only the single collapsed chain, never the matrix re-expressed row-by-row (that would violate the one-chain-per-conclusion rule above). An exact tie between weighted totals still resolves to a single named recommended option; a tie must not produce a multi-option chain endpoint. **Exact-tie tiebreak (deterministic):** on an exact tie, prefer the option with fewer `GT-N?` (unverified) inputs among its winning criteria; if still tied, name both totals in the chain intermediate but select the first-listed option as the chain endpoint, and flag the tie explicitly in the Conclusion section's confidence line.
332	
333	**Second-order effect list → order-marked extension.** A second-order effect list extends the parent chain IN PLACE as additional order-marked steps, each carrying the same evidentiary discipline as the first-order steps that produced the conclusion:
334	
335	```text
336	GT-N → first-order conclusion →[2nd] [2nd-order effect] →[3rd] [3rd-order effect] (contradicts GT-M → back to Phase 2)
337	```
338	
339	Example: `GT-1 → first-order conclusion →[2nd] flag-config surface grows →[3rd] flag debt accumulates (contradicts GT-4 → back to P2)`. The order marks (`[2nd]`, `[3rd]`) make the extension's sequence legible. A contradicting effect routes the conclusion back to Phase 2 — never directly to Phase 3 or past Phase 2. A pass that surfaces no non-contradicting downstream effect leaves the parent chain unextended — a clean no-op, not an error.
340	
341	### Confidence levels, defined
342	
343	`HIGH`, `MEDIUM` and `LOW` name how much of a chain is **outstanding** — not how strongly the analysis believes its conclusion. Three axes decide the band, each answerable by inspecting what the chain already carries on the page:
344	
345	- **Inputs** — the provenance of every identifier on the head line: an unsuffixed `GT-N` with a named read-at-source location, a `?`-marked ground truth, or a `Cn` carrying its own band.
346	- **Inference** — whether each hop the chain's endpoint depends on follows from the line above it, or needs a premise supplied by an `[Assumes: A-N]` annotation.
347	- **Rivals** — whether a competing conclusion from the same ground truths survives, and what rules it out. Section 5 is where the ruling-out is written down, so a chain answers this axis by pointing at its own Abandoned Reasoning entry as readily as by carrying the rival on its confidence line.
348	
349	**The band is the lowest the three axes license.** A chain is not HIGH because two of them are clean.
350	
351	**HIGH — nothing on this chain is outstanding.** Every identifier on the head line is an unsuffixed `GT-N` whose read-at-source location is named, or a `Cn` itself rated HIGH; every hop the endpoint depends on follows from the line above it by deduction, by arithmetic that recomputes when redone independently of the chain text, or by a regularity cited to an unsuffixed ground truth; and the strongest rival conclusion the analysis considered is named — on this confidence line or in a section 5 entry this chain points to — together with the ground truth or chain that rules it out, that ruling-out input itself unsuffixed. A chain whose endpoint a live alternative still contests is unexamined, not certain: it is MEDIUM at best.
352	
353	An `[Assumes: A-N]` annotation on a hop shorts the Inference axis **unless** the confidence line says what becomes of the endpoint when that assumption fails and the endpoint still stands — *"A2 is that the CDN'd assets are versioned; if they were not, the CDN result would be weaker evidence still, so the conclusion is unaffected"*. An annotation on a hop that only qualifies a second-order extension, and not the endpoint, is outside this axis and the chain says which case it is. Stating the sensitivity is the work; an unexamined assumption is not the same thing as one whose falsity has been priced.
354	
355	The Rivals axis is answered when a section 5 entry names a competing conclusion to this chain's endpoint and the chain or ground truth that ruled it out, or when the endpoint is itself a ruling-out — a chain establishing that some option does not work has already done the rival's work and does not need a rival of its own. It is short when a competing conclusion has been raised anywhere in the analysis and nothing settles it, and when the analysis reaches a positive recommendation with no section 5 content bearing on it at all.
356	
357	**MEDIUM — exactly one axis is short, and the shortfall is named and bounded.** One of: an identifier on the head line is `?`-marked or is a `Cn` rated MEDIUM; or at most one hop the endpoint depends on rests on a stated `[Assumes: A-N]` premise whose failure the chain has not priced; or a rival to the endpoint is live and nothing in the analysis settles it. The confidence line names which axis is short, names the specific input, hop or rival, and states what would close it — the verification that would remove an input as a cause of the downgrade, the evidence that would establish an assumed premise, or the observation that would settle between this conclusion and its rival. A MEDIUM chain is one whose weakness a reader can point at.
358	
359	**LOW — the shortfall is unbounded, or more than one axis is short.** Two or more axes short at once; or an input is `?` with no verification path available; or a hop's missing premise cannot be stated as an assumption at all, so the analysis cannot say what would make the step valid; or a rival survives that no available observation would settle. A LOW chain is reportable, and a conclusion resting on it alone is not actionable.
360	
361	**Calibration rule.** Each rating is the highest its inputs, hops and rivals license, **and no higher**. Rating above what the axes license over-claims. Rating below it is a defect of the same kind: a chain meeting HIGH on all three axes and written MEDIUM misreports the analysis's own strength, and a document whose every chain carries the same defensive band tells a reader nothing about which parts to trust. Criterion 5 scores calibration, not altitude — an analysis whose every band is the one its axes license is Rigorous whether its conclusion is HIGH, MEDIUM or LOW.
362	
363	**The caps are consequences, not extra rules.** The unverified-input rule (D-07) below and the ceiling at the lowest-rated chain a head cites are what the Inputs axis says, restated for the two cases that occur most often; they are the fast check, and these definitions are what they check for. A cap never licenses a band on its own — it bounds from above, and the band is still the lowest any of the three axes licenses.
364	
365	**Confidence pre-check (Inputs axis).** Directly above every `**Confidence:**` line — each §4 chain's and the §6 Conclusion's — write one `**Pre-check:**` line, with nothing between it and the `**Confidence:**` line it checks:
366	
367	```text
368	**Pre-check:** head GT-1, GT-3?, C2 (MEDIUM) · ?-marked: GT-3? · lowest cited: MEDIUM · Inputs ceiling: MEDIUM
369	**Confidence:** MEDIUM — GT-3? is unverified; …
370	```
371	
372	Four fields, separated by ` · `: `head` lists every identifier on the chain's head line (the part before the first `→`), in order, comma-separated, a `?` suffix kept (`GT-3?`), each `Cn` followed by its own stated band in parentheses (`C2 (MEDIUM)`) — for the §6 roll-up, `head` is every chain the Conclusion rests on, each with its band, plus any `GT-N?` the Conclusion rests on directly. `?-marked` lists the `?`-suffixed identifiers from `head`, comma-separated, or the token `none`. `lowest cited` is the lowest band among the `Cn` in `head`, or `none` when `head` cites no chain. `Inputs ceiling` is the Inputs axis's bound: `LOW` if `lowest cited` is LOW; otherwise `MEDIUM` if `?-marked` is not `none` or `lowest cited` is MEDIUM; otherwise `HIGH`.
373	
374	This is the Inputs axis of "Confidence levels, defined" made procedural — Inference and Rivals are not scored on this line, and can only lower the band further. The ceiling bounds from above, as the caps-are-consequences paragraph above states; the `**Confidence:**` label may equal it or sit below it, and never above it — a below-ceiling label is explained by the Confidence line itself, not by the pre-check. In §6, the pre-check line is itself a Conclusion-section claim under the Claim inventory rule below, and it is cited by the chains its own `head` names.
375	
376	### Conclusion C1: [Conclusion text]
377	
378	GT-N ([brief fact label, source]) + GT-M ([brief fact label, source])
379	→ [intermediate claim — a new inference statable from combining GT-N and GT-M but from neither alone]
380	→ [conclusion — the claim this chain establishes]
381	
382	**Pre-check:** head [every head identifier; each Cn with its band, e.g. C2 (MEDIUM)] · ?-marked: [the GT-N? identifiers, or none] · lowest cited: [lowest Cn band, or none] · Inputs ceiling: [HIGH / MEDIUM / LOW]
383	**Confidence:** [HIGH / MEDIUM / LOW]
384	[If MEDIUM or LOW: name each GT-N? input with the verification that would remove it as a cause of the downgrade; name each Cn on this chain's head rated below HIGH, which need not be re-explained here; and give each downgrade cause belonging to this chain itself — for example a weak inference step or an absent-fails derivation — with what would remove it as a cause of the downgrade or a stated reason no verification path exists (the validation-rubric absent-fails EXCEPT clause, for an absent-fails derivation, or an explicit account of why no available evidence settles that cause).]
385	
386	**Unverified input rule (D-07):** A chain that includes any `GT-N?` input must end with a MEDIUM or LOW confidence line. The line must name the unverified input and state the verification that would remove it as a cause of the downgrade. A HIGH confidence claim cannot rest on an unverified ground truth. 309	**Provenance check (apply before banding).** A citation being present is not verification. For

325	  by that record naming which source and why unreachable.

379	intermediate step — **and** the **Abandoned Reasoning** section (output section 5).

Quoted span: where the band is determined by chain form or chain dependency, it must be drawn from the self-audit scan's chain-form table row or rows that determine the band, not from the Derivation Chains prose directly. Where the band is determined by the Abandoned Reasoning section, the no-analogies-as-direct-evidence ban, a missing `[Assumes: X]` declaration, or hop validity and arithmetic — none of which the chain-form table carries a column for — quote the analysis text directly. Folds in:
381	dead-end honesty, the no-analogies-as-direct-evidence ban (D-07), escape-valve policing for Abandoned
382	Reasoning (D-03), and hop validity and arithmetic. The one-line form is the degenerate case, used only when the whole chain fits on one physical line; a chain that does not fit uses the head-plus-arrow-led form, and a hop is split rather than continued on a second line.

385	  has exactly one derivation chain in section 4; each chain names the inputs it consumes — ground truths, upstream conclusions, or both — in the prescribed head form (`GT-1? ([brief fact label]) + C2 ([brief fact label])`),
386	  contains at least one intermediate claim (a claim that cannot be stated from any single named input alone), and reaches a conclusion; each chain is rendered in the prescribed
387	  arrow-led form. A hop occupies exactly one physical line. Every line after the head begins with `→` and carries exactly one complete hop; a hop is never broken across physical lines. The head line lists the inputs the chain consumes: each is a `GT-N` identifier (`GT-N?` when the ground truth is unverified) or a `Cn` identifier, optionally followed by a parenthesized gloss, joined to the next by `+`. The first `→` closes the head. An input carrying unparenthesized prose — `C2's threshold` — is not an identifier and does not parse; write `C2 (threshold)` in every position. The mechanical form check detects that violation only when the prose input is the last one before the first `→`; in an earlier position the check matches the well-formed remainder and scores the head conforming, so the rule binds in positions the check does not reach. The head grammar governs the head line only. A hop is prose: `C2's saving` is fine after the first `→`, and is not an input reference. One exception: a hop must not begin with a `GT-N` identifier, which the form check reads as the head of a new chain and which therefore ends this one — write `→ the duty cycle stated in GT-4 is the binding term`, not `→ GT-4's stated duty cycle is the binding term`. The form check detects that violation only while fewer than two hops precede it; in a later position the check matches the preceding hops and scores the chain conforming, so the rule binds in positions the check does not reach. The mechanical form check additionally rejects a chain whose head or first hop closes its own sentence before the next `→`: it reads the following arrow-led line as a new statement and ends the chain there, so a chain satisfying every rule above is scored malformed for that reason alone. The check reaches only that position — a hop that closes its own sentence from the second hop onward does not change the verdict — which is why intermediate hops carry no terminal punctuation in this project's worked examples. Hops rendered as an ordered list do not satisfy the prescribed form; the Abandoned Reasoning

## Adversarial pass (process output)

**Recompute.** The trade-off weighted-score table (§4, feeding C6) is recomputed independently of the chain prose, weights = [Cert 5, RealWorld 4, Feedback 3, Equity 4, Cost 3, Misuse 4]:
- A (pure timed): 5×5 + 4×2 + 3×3 + 4×2 + 3×5 + 4×5 = 25+8+9+8+15+20 = **85** (matches).
- B (pure unsupervised take-home): 5×1 + 4×5 + 3×2 + 4×3 + 3×3 + 4×1 = 5+20+6+12+9+4 = **56** (matches).
- C (take-home + mandatory universal oral defense): 5×5 + 4×4 + 3×3 + 4×3 + 3×2 + 4×5 = 25+16+9+12+6+20 = **88** (matches).
- D (hybrid — recommended): 5×5 + 4×5 + 3×4 + 4×4 + 3×4 + 4×5 = 25+20+12+16+12+20 = **105** (matches).
- E (in-class AI-inclusive timed exam alone): 5×4 + 4×4 + 3×3 + 4×3 + 3×4 + 4×5 = 20+16+9+12+12+20 = **89**.
  A first-pass draft of this analysis stated E's total as 101; independent recomputation here finds **89**, not 101 — the draft figure was an arithmetic error and is corrected in §4's chain C6 and in this record. The corrected ranking (D=105 > E=89 > C=88 > A=85 > B=56) leaves the headline recommendation (D dominates) unchanged, because the dominance argument is componentwise (see Sensitivity below), not total-dependent — but the error is disclosed rather than silently fixed.

**Sensitivity.** The single ground truth whose falsity would most plausibly flip the recommendation is **GT-1?** (AI-text detectors are unreliable — 12–26% false-positive rate on human text, near-0% accuracy on hybrid human-AI text). It is `?`-marked: two direct-read attempts were made this session (arXiv 2608.11256 — PDF content not extractable via fetch; Springer 10.1007/s40979-026-00213-1 — redirected to an institutional-auth wall, not followed) and both failed; see the Ground Truths section for the Phase 3 failure records. If GT-1 were false — i.e., if AI-authorship detection were in fact reliable (sub-1% error, robust across domains and hybrid text) — pure unsupervised take-home (option B) would no longer be knocked out on the Certification criterion, its weighted score would rise sharply, and it could overtake D. This exact condition is named as this analysis's stated Falsification condition below. The weakest link per chain: C1 — the five-function framing is taken from the question's own scope, not independently re-derived; C2 — rests on GT-1's currently-unread figures; C3 — rests on a single 60-student preference study (GT-10?) for generalizability; C4 — rests on an unpiloted assumption (A-16) about grade-weight thresholds; C5 — rests on an unmeasured magnitude for paid-AI-tier disparity (A-5); C6 — inherits C2/C3/C5's weakest links plus analyst-assigned (though pre-locked) trade-off weights.

**Rival.** Headline conclusion (adopt hybrid D): the strongest rival is "AI-authorship-verification technology will mature soon (behavioral biometrics, process-replay, cryptographic provenance), making unsupervised take-home (B) fully defensible and the whole hybrid an unneeded transitional complexity." This is **not ruled out** by this analysis — no evidence of a mature, production-scale, non-detector verification technology was found this session — so it is carried live as the Falsification condition rather than dismissed; see Abandoned Reasoning entry 6. Intermediate chains: **C1** — rival not applicable — no alternative framing was found that avoids the objective-specific conclusion without contradicting GT-11 or GT-12. **C2** — rival is the same detection-improves rival named above; not ruled out, carried to Falsification. **C3** — rival not applicable — no competing account of construct validity for tool-available work was identified. **C4** — rival: "closed-book timed exams remain the best predictor of durable competence, so real-world-validity (C3) should be subordinated to retention (C4), not merely supplemented by it" — this rival is **partially incorporated, not ruled out**: C6's hybrid retains a graded checkpoint-exam component specifically because of C4, rather than overriding it (see Abandoned Reasoning entry 2 for the fully-timed alternative this stops short of). **C5** — rival: "take-home's equity harms (unequal home environment, unequal paid-tool access) exceed timed format's equity harms (accommodable disability burden) in aggregate, so timed format is more equitable overall" — **live, not ruled out**; no comparative-magnitude data was found this session, so this is carried into §6 as an explicit local-context trigger condition rather than resolved.

**Premise.** The hybrid policy (chain C6) has already failed: three years after adoption, faculty report the architecture as worse than either pure format, and employers report the credential is less legible than before.

**Causes (unfiltered, generated from student / faculty / employer-accreditor viewpoints, written before grouping):**
1. (student) Spot-check oral defenses feel arbitrary — "why was I picked and not them" — generating grievance complaints.
2. (student) AI-inclusive timed checkpoints degrade into "memorize the AI's typical phrasing" rather than testing genuine competence.
3. (student) Students with premium AI subscriptions and private oral-defense coaching outperform peers — a new equity gap opens exactly where the old one was supposedly closed.
4. (student) Lightly-graded retrieval checks still register as "one more high-stakes test," raising net stress above either pure format.
5. (student) Ambiguous AI-use disclosure norms ("how much help is allowed?") create anxiety and inconsistent enforcement across sections and graders.
6. (faculty) No new grading budget is allocated; instructors quietly let the oral spot-check sampling rate drift toward zero under time pressure, silently defeating the authorship backstop.
7. (faculty) Rubrics for "AI-inclusive" work are never actually rewritten, so graders inconsistently penalize any visible AI involvement, contradicting the stated policy.
8. (faculty) Grading-load increases concentrate on junior/adjunct faculty, who have the least power to push back, concentrating burnout where it is least sustainable.
9. (employer/accreditor) An external licensure body does not recognize the hybrid pathway as equivalent, forcing a costly parallel proctored track anyway and negating the hoped-for cost savings.
10. (employer/accreditor) Employers, reading a transcript, cannot tell which grades reflect individually-verified competence versus tool-assisted competence — undermining the credential's signaling value, the opposite of the policy's goal.

**Clusters (structural weaknesses):**
- **Cluster 1 — Deterrence collapse under resource pressure** (causes 1, 4, 6, 7). The risk-based oral spot-check is the single point of failure for the entire authorship-verification claim; if its sampling rate silently drops under an unfunded mandate, C2's certification-validity claim collapses toward option B's low Certification score. Bears on: C2, C6, A-14 (faculty resourcing), A-17 (deterrence-economics parameter).
- **Cluster 2 — A new equity gap replaces the old one** (cause 3). Oral-defense/coaching-access disparity was not modeled in the C5 equity trade-off, which compared home-environment/paid-tool disparities against accommodation burden but not against coaching-access disparity. Bears on: C5.
- **Cluster 3 — Credential illegibility to external parties** (causes 9, 10). A merged hybrid grade does not communicate which components were individually-certified versus tool-assisted, undermining the "fair ranking / certification" function even if the internal policy logic is sound. Bears on: C2, C6, and the Essence Statement's success criteria.
- **Cluster 4 — Ambiguous norms, inconsistent enforcement** (causes 2, 5). The recommendation as drafted underspecifies a disclosure-tier standard. Bears on: C6 (an implementation gap, not a chain contradiction).

**Disposition:**
- Cluster 1 — **Plan change:** the oral/process spot-check sampling rate is made a published, audited policy floor (proposed default: ≥20% of take-home submissions plus 100% of grade-boundary and AI-detector-flagged-anomaly cases), funded explicitly in the department's resourcing plan and reported annually to the chair/provost — not left to individual-instructor discretion. Added to §6.
- Cluster 2 — **Plan change + accepted residual risk:** structure spot-checks as short, rubric-anchored, binary pass/fail ("authorship confirmed" / "not confirmed") rather than a scored oral performance, reducing the advantage coachable eloquence provides; pilot for demographic score gaps before full rollout. Residual risk accepted: some coaching-access advantage may remain; mitigated by the binary (not graded) design.
- Cluster 3 — **Plan change:** transcripts and course descriptions explicitly label which grade components were individually-certified (in-room checkpoint) versus tool-assisted (take-home/project), rather than merging them into one opaque grade. Added to §6.
- Cluster 4 — **Plan change:** adopt a single university-level AI-use disclosure rubric with named tiers (e.g., Tier 0 — no AI; Tier 1 — AI-assisted, cited; Tier 2 — AI-primary, verified), published before each term starts, rather than leaving it to per-instructor discretion. Added to §6.

**Falsification.** This analysis's conclusion (adopt the hybrid architecture D over pure A, B, C, or E) is false if: (a) a reliable, independently-audited, low-cost AI-authorship-verification method (sub-1% false-positive and false-negative rate, robust to hybrid human-AI text) becomes available and standard — which would remove B's Certification-criterion penalty and could overtake D; or (b) a controlled study finds no significant difference in professional/licensure outcomes between hybrid-D graduates and pure-A graduates, which would remove the rationale for D's added complexity over A for licensure-bound programs; or (c) the oral-spot-check backstop is shown, empirically, to introduce equity harms (e.g., language-fluency or coaching-access bias) larger than the ones it was adopted to fix.
FP_EOF

### Inversion procedure (Phase 2 companion technique)

**Claim inverted:** "A well-designed assessment policy will maintain both learning integrity and real-world relevance as AI capability grows" → inverted to "the policy fails to maintain both."

## 3. Ground Truths

- **GT-1?** Commercial/independent AI-text detectors show high, inconsistent accuracy: best-case published false-positive rates near 1-2% on curated academic writing, but independent 2025-2026 evaluations find 12-26% false-positive rates on human-written text generally, false-positive rates exceeding 20% for non-native English writers, and accuracy dropping to near 0% on hybrid human-AI text — cited to: Springer/Booth (2025), Sultan Qaboos University (2026), arXiv 2608.11256 ("Why AI Detection Fails for Academic Integrity," Karr/Khvatskii/Hua/Chawla), GradPilot, Hastewire, ProofAcademic aggregated via WebSearch; reported-by-delegate: WebSearch result summaries — cited sources not opened successfully by this analysis. **Phase 3 failure record:** two direct-read attempts made — (1) arXiv 2608.11256 PDF fetched but content not extractable (encoding); (2) Springer 10.1007/s40979-026-00213-1 fetch redirected to an institutional-authorization wall and was not followed. Both failures are disclosed; GT-1 remains `?`.
- **GT-2** At Birkbeck Law School, after reintroducing invigilated in-person exams, "more than 45 per cent" of students received a first-class grading, versus "13 per cent" the prior year under take-home essays — source: Times Higher Education, "Are universities returning to in-person exams to combat AI cheating?"; read-at-source: fetched directly, figures quoted verbatim from the article's institutional-changes section.
- **GT-3** A UK freedom-of-information analysis found 78% of UK universities still using online (unproctored/take-home-style) exams; of those, 65% used no proctoring service, 70% had no plans to phase out online exams, 19% intended to scale back, and 3% (two institutions) planned complete elimination — source: Times Higher Education (same article); read-at-source: fetched directly, figures quoted verbatim.
- **GT-4** Student AI use in studies rose from 66% to 95% year-over-year in the most recent cited survey, and the share of students including AI-generated text directly in assessed submissions rose from 3% to 12% over the same period — source: Times Higher Education (same article, citing HEPI survey data); read-at-source: fetched directly, figures quoted verbatim.
- **GT-5?** In Roediger & Karpicke's (2006) testing-effect experiments, repeated retrieval-practice testing produced higher one-week-delayed recall than repeated rereading (61% vs. 40%), though repeated restudying outperformed testing at a 5-minute delay — cited to: Roediger & Karpicke (2006), *Perspectives on Psychological Science*; reported-by-delegate: WebSearch result summary — cited source not opened by this analysis.
- **GT-6?** Only 11% of students, asked open-endedly about study techniques, spontaneously report using retrieval practice — cited to: retrieval-practice literature review aggregated via WebSearch; reported-by-delegate — cited source not opened by this analysis.
- **GT-7?** US workplace AI use ("a few times a year" or more) rose from 40% to 45% between Q2 and Q3 2025; daily use is roughly 10%; only 37% of employees report their employer has formally implemented AI for productivity — cited to: Gallup workplace AI survey (2025); reported-by-delegate: WebSearch result summary — cited source not opened by this analysis.
- **GT-8** Current LLM-based AI writing assistants (Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini, as of this analysis's Jan-2026 knowledge cutoff) are capable, for a large class of standard university writing/analysis assignments (essays, problem sets, literature reviews, code), of producing a complete first-draft response meeting or exceeding typical passing-grade quality within minutes, without the student having mastered the underlying material — provenance: definitional/directly observable — this analysis is itself an instance of such a tool; no external citation required; read-at-source: n/a (analytic claim, verifiable by inspection of the named tools' documented capabilities).
- **GT-9** Federal law (ADA, Section 504) requires that testing entities administer exams so that scores "accurately reflect the individual's aptitude, achievement level, or the skill that the exam purports to measure, rather than the individual's impairment," which in practice requires reasonable accommodation (e.g., extended time) for documented disabilities on timed exams — but does not require eliminating timed formats — source: ADA.gov, "ADA Requirements: Testing Accommodations"; read-at-source: fetched directly, quoted verbatim.
- **GT-10?** Authentic/portfolio assessment shows greater construct validity for measuring real-world professional competence than closed-book exams, and a comparative study of 60 university engineering students found students overwhelmingly preferred portfolio assessment over exams, citing reduced test anxiety and better alignment with professional demands — cited to: authentic-assessment literature review, ScienceDirect systematic review (2024), and a named 60-student engineering comparative study, aggregated via WebSearch; reported-by-delegate — cited sources not opened by this analysis.
- **GT-11** A timed, in-person, invigilated, closed-device written exam is, by construction, the one format in which the artifact is produced entirely within a bounded window under direct observation, making the causal link between "who produced this artifact" and "the enrolled student" verifiable by direct observation — provenance: definitional/logical entailment of "in-person" + "invigilated" + "closed-device"; no external citation required; read-at-source: n/a (analytic claim).
- **GT-12** A take-home assessment completed unsupervised, on a personal device, with no technical restriction on tool use, cannot — from the artifact alone — verify that the submitting student (rather than another person or an AI system) produced the intellectual content, absent an additional verification mechanism, given GT-1's documented detector unreliability and GT-8's documented AI capability — provenance: logical entailment of GT-1 + GT-8 + the absence of direct observation; no independent external citation required; read-at-source: n/a (analytic claim, inherits GT-1's `?` as an input but is not itself an independent empirical claim).
- **GT-13?** US professional licensure examinations that gate entry to regulated professions (e.g., the bar examination's two-day format with the Multistate Bar Examination component; the USMLE for medical licensure) remain proctored, standardized, center-based or otherwise directly-observed assessments, independent of any individual university's own coursework assessment policy — cited to: American Bar Association bar-admissions resources, USMLE program materials, aggregated via WebSearch; reported-by-delegate — cited sources not opened by this analysis; not read this session — turn budget (prioritized GT-1 and GT-9 for direct-source verification instead, since GT-13 is not load-bearing for the headline architecture-dominance finding — see chain C6's Pre-check).

## 4. Derivation Chains

### Conclusion C1: "Replace timed exams with take-home" is the wrong frame; the right frame is objective-specific assessment design.

→ detection software cannot serve as a reliable backstop for verifying who produced an unsupervised take-home artifact

→ for assessment components whose function is producing or evaluating quality work using available tools, a closed-book timed exam under-measures the target competence because it forbids the tools that competence is defined around

→ this degrades durable foundational retention even while C3's target competence continues to be measured well *[Assumes: A-16 — retrieval-practice checks must carry nonzero grade weight to be used, since ungraded practice is skipped at roughly the same low voluntary-adoption rate GT-6 documents]*

### Trade-off analysis (companion technique, feeding chain C6)

**Options** (status quo named explicitly, per the procedure): (A) pure timed in-person exam — status quo; (B) pure unsupervised take-home, unrestricted AI use; (C) take-home with mandatory universal oral defense of every artifact; (D) hybrid — in-room timed AI-inclusive checkpoint exams for certifiable competence + take-home/project work for extended synthesis + risk-based (not universal) oral/process spot-check backstop; (E) in-class AI-inclusive timed exam alone (open-tool, in-room, proctored, no take-home component).

**Must-haves (knockouts, applied before scoring):** (i) must satisfy external licensure/accreditation floors where applicable (GT-13?) — knocks out B as a *sole, universal* policy for licensure-bound programs. (ii) must not require an infeasible faculty grading-load increase without added resourcing at large enrollment (A-6, A-14) — knocks out C as a *mandatory, universal* requirement above roughly 150-200 students; C survives only as the bounded, risk-sampled form, which is exactly what D already is.

**Criteria, weights (1-5, locked before scoring), and anchors:**
1. Certification validity (weight 5) — 1 = no authorship verification possible; 5 = fully verified by direct observation.
2. Real-world/construct validity (weight 4) — 1 = prohibits realistic tool use; 5 = fully mirrors professional tool-available conditions.
3. Formative feedback / durable-learning motivation (weight 3) — 1 = no retrieval-practice element; 5 = strong built-in retrieval practice (GT-5?, GT-6?).
4. Equity (weight 4) — 1 = large uncontrolled disparities; 5 = disparities minimized/mitigated (GT-9, A-5).
5. Faculty cost/scalability (weight 3) — 1 = infeasible at scale without major new resources; 5 = scales with existing resources (A-6, A-14).
6. Resistance to undetectable AI misuse at scale (weight 4) — 1 = fully vulnerable; 5 = robust regardless of the detector arms race (GT-1?).

**Scores and weighted totals** (recomputed and verified in the Adversarial pass above):

| Option | Cert(5) | RealWorld(4) | Feedback(3) | Equity(4) | Cost(3) | Misuse(4) | Weighted total |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| A — pure timed | 5 | 2 | 3 | 2 | 5 | 5 | 85 |
| B — pure unsupervised take-home | 1 | 5 | 2 | 3 | 3 | 1 | 56 |
| C — take-home + universal oral defense | 5 | 4 | 3 | 3 | 2 | 5 | 88 |
| D — hybrid (recommended) | 5 | 5 | 4 | 4 | 4 | 5 | **105** |
| E — in-class AI-inclusive timed exam alone | 4 | 4 | 3 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 89 |

**Flip test:** D's score vector [5,5,4,4,4,5] is componentwise ≥ every rival option's vector on every one of the six criteria (ties only on Cert vs. C, and on Misuse vs. C/E) — D weakly Pareto-dominates every alternative. A dominance relation that holds componentwise cannot be reversed by any reweighting of positive weights, so **no single-criterion weight change flips the winner**; this is a stronger result than the standard flip-distance report and is stated as such rather than manufacturing a flip-distance number that does not exist.

### Second-order thinking (companion technique, mandatory per Phase 4 exit criterion — extends the hybrid recommendation before Phase 5)

**Actor lens:** *Students* adapt: if summative stakes shift toward take-home, students will lean harder on AI there and may skip low-stakes retrieval checks unless those checks carry real grade weight (confirms A-16 is load-bearing, not decorative — see C4). *Faculty* adapt: grading load shifts from fast-to-grade formats toward take-home/project grading plus oral spot-checks; without added resourcing, faculty will quietly under-deliver the spot-check component (this is exactly Pre-mortem Cluster 1, below). *Employers* adapt: rising workplace AI use (GT-7?) means employers increasingly expect AI-augmented-workflow fluency; a degree that never assesses it risks signaling stale skills, which is competitive pressure reinforcing C3's direction over time. *Adversarial actors* (contract-cheating/AI-ghostwriting services) adapt: as take-home stakes rise without a verification backstop, the incentive to outsource rises proportionally — meaning the oral/process spot-check (C6, below) is load-bearing for the hybrid to hold under adversarial pressure at scale, not an optional add-on.

**Time lens:** *Immediate* (this term): transition friction — rubrics must be rewritten to define what "showing your own reasoning" means under AI-inclusive assessment. *A few cycles* (2-4 semesters): the AI-detection arms race continues to favor students/AI over detectors (GT-1?'s trend direction), so any design still relying on detection software as a primary defense degrades further — reinforcing that the hybrid's backstop must be process/oral-based, not detector-based. *Long run* (beyond this analysis's Jan-2026 knowledge cutoff): the boundary of "what only an unaided human can do" keeps shrinking as AI capability improves, so today's specific "foundational competence" checkpoint content will itself need periodic redefinition — this is why §6 recommends a scheduled review/sunset clause (A-15) rather than a fixed, permanent policy.

**Contradiction check:** none of the above second-order effects contradicts a Ground Truth; the extension proceeds to Conclusion C6 below without looping back to Phase 2.

### Conclusion C6: Adopt the hybrid architecture (option D) as the default assessment policy; treat "replace timed exams with take-home" as a false binary.

GT-1? (AI detectors unreliable) + GT-13? (licensure-bound programs require proctored components) + C1 (right frame is objective-specific) + C2 (certification needs observed production where required) + C3 (take-home superior for the real-world-validity function) + C5 (equity needs mitigation, not format choice)
→ scoring five candidate assessment architectures against six weighted, evidence-anchored criteria (recomputed in the Adversarial pass) shows the hybrid architecture scoring at or above every rival architecture on every single criterion, a dominance result robust to any single-criterion reweighting
→ pure unsupervised take-home is knocked out wherever unaided individual certification is a stated function, and mandatory universal oral defense is knocked out at large enrollment without added resourcing, but a risk-based sampled oral/process spot-check avoids both knockouts while still backstopping authorship, provided it is funded and its second-order adversarial-incentive risk (named above) is priced into the policy rather than ignored
→ the hybrid architecture is therefore the recommended default policy, with a directly-observed, individually-certifying floor fixed wherever external licensure or accreditation bodies require it, independent of the university's own pedagogical preference

## 5. Abandoned Reasoning

### Dead End 1: Ban AI outright and rely on AI-text-detection software as the enforcement mechanism

**What was tried:** Treating detector-based enforcement as the primary integrity mechanism for any take-home component, on the assumption (A-1) that detection is reliable enough to backstop authorship.

**Why abandoned:** Contradicted by GT-1? — independent evaluations show 12-26% false-positive rates on human-written text, over 20% false-positive rates for non-native English writers, and near-0% accuracy on hybrid human-AI text. A mechanism with this error profile cannot be the basis of a high-stakes integrity determination.

**What it ruled out:** Any policy design (including several early real-world university responses documented in GT-4) that treats a detector score as authoritative evidence of misconduct; this is why chain C2 and the trade-off's Misuse-resistance criterion define "robust" as "not dependent on detector accuracy."

### Dead End 2: Full return to 100% timed, in-person, closed-book exams for everything

**What was tried:** Treating the pre-AI status quo (option A, universally applied) as the default-safe answer, motivated by GT-2's grade-inflation data point.

**Why abandoned:** Ruled out by chain C3 and GT-7? — most modern knowledge work is now tool-augmented, so a closed-book format under-measures the "produce quality work with available tools" competence entirely, failing the real-world-preparation function named in the original scope.

**What it ruled out:** Treating C4's retention-preservation finding as license to override C3 rather than supplement it — the hybrid (C6) retains a checkpoint-exam component specifically because of C4, without reverting to 100% closed-book coverage.

### Dead End 3: Full replacement with unrestricted, unsupervised take-home assessment for everything

**What was tried:** Treating AI-tool availability (GT-7?, GT-8) as sufficient justification for eliminating all directly-observed assessment.

**Why abandoned:** Ruled out by chain C2 — GT-12's authorship-unverifiability problem, combined with GT-1?'s detector unreliability, means the "certify individual unaided competence" function becomes undeliverable under this design wherever that function is actually required (e.g., licensure-adjacent coursework, GT-13?).

**What it ruled out:** Treating "AI tools exist and are useful" as a complete argument for format choice on its own — GT-8 alone does not resolve which function a given assessment component needs to serve.

### Dead End 4: Universal, mandatory oral defense of every submitted artifact

**What was tried:** Considered as the strongest single mechanism for closing the authorship-verification gap without relying on detectors, applied to 100% of take-home submissions.

**Why abandoned:** Assumption A-6/A-14 (faculty grading capacity) makes this infeasible at scale — the trade-off's must-have knockout rules out option C as a *universal* requirement above roughly 150-200 enrolled students, absent new resourcing that this analysis found no evidence is typically provided.

**What it ruled out:** A "universal oral defense" policy as the whole solution; retained only in bounded, risk-based, funded form inside the hybrid (C6), which is what avoids the knockout that felled the universal version.

### Dead End 5: Treating GT-2's Birkbeck 45%/13% grade jump as proof that take-home grades were AI-inflated and therefore invalid

**What was tried:** Using the Birkbeck first-class-grading swing directly as evidence that take-home assessment specifically produces inflated, unreliable grades under AI availability.

**Why abandoned:** This is one plausible reading but not the only one — grading-calibration differences between in-person and take-home rubrics, or a cohort effect, are equally consistent with the same single data point, and no controlled comparison was found this session to distinguish them. Treating it as proof would over-claim beyond what GT-2 (read at source, but a single institutional anecdote) can support.

**What it ruled out:** Using GT-2 as a load-bearing input in any derivation chain; it is retained in §3 only as illustrative, motivating context for why universities are reconsidering take-home formats, not as evidence inside C1-C6.

### Dead End 6: Treating "AI-authorship-verification technology will mature soon, making the hybrid unnecessary" as already-resolved (either accepted or dismissed)

**What was tried:** Considering whether to build the recommendation around an assumption that non-detector verification technology (behavioral biometrics, process-replay, cryptographic provenance) will mature within the policy's planning horizon.

**Why abandoned:** No evidence of a mature, production-scale, independently-audited technology of this kind was found this session — but its future arrival cannot be ruled out either. Treating it as resolved in either direction would overstate this analysis's evidence.

**What it ruled out:** A permanent, unconditional recommendation; instead, this exact condition is carried forward as this analysis's explicit Falsification condition (§5 Adversarial pass, above) and as trigger condition 1 in §6.

### Dead End 7: Deriving the oral/process spot-check sampling-rate floor (≥20%) from a formal Fermi/deterrence-economics estimate

**What was tried:** Attempting to compute a specific sampling-rate floor from first-principles unit-factors (probability of AI misuse × penalty severity × effort saved), per the estimate (Fermi) companion technique.

**Why abandoned:** No reliable unit-factor data was available in this analysis for any of the three factors (no measured distribution of AI-use-for-cheating probability, no standard penalty-severity scale, no measured effort-hours saved per assignment type) — fabricating such factors would produce false precision rather than a defensible estimate. See the Techniques-not-applied block above.

**What it ruled out:** Presenting ≥20% as an empirically-derived figure; it is instead presented in §6 explicitly as a design parameter requiring local calibration, carrying the `no chain — flagged assumption only` marker.

## 6. Conclusion

**Recommended approach:** Do not "replace" timed in-person exams with take-home assessments as a blanket university policy. Adopt a hybrid architecture instead: in-room, timed, AI-inclusive checkpoint exams for the subset of competence a course must individually certify, take-home/project work (with disclosed AI use) for the subset whose function is producing high-quality work with available tools, and a risk-based — not universal — oral or process spot-check as an authorship backstop on high-stakes take-home components (chain C6).

**Key insight:** "Should take-home replace timed exams" is a category error, not a genuinely contingent question with one right global answer — the five assessment functions named in the original scope (certification, motivation, feedback, ranking, real-world prep) systematically favor opposite formats, so treating format choice as a single university-wide switch guarantees under-serving at least one function no matter which way the switch is thrown (chain C1).

**Trade-offs acknowledged:**
- Retrieval-practice checks must carry nonzero grade weight to preserve durable learning under this policy; this is the analysis's lowest-confidence finding and should be piloted, not assumed (chain C4).
- Equity requires explicit, funded mitigations regardless of which format a course uses (chain C5).
- Which format is more equitable in aggregate for a given institution is not determined by this analysis, for lack of comparative-magnitude data on home-environment/paid-tool disparity versus accommodation burden — no chain — flagged assumption only.
- The proposed oral/process spot-check sampling floor (≥20%) is a design parameter set by judgment, not a validated deterrence-economics figure — no chain — flagged assumption only.

**Additional required design features:**
- Publish and fund a minimum oral/process spot-check sampling rate as an audited policy floor (proposed default ≥20% of take-home submissions, plus 100% of grade-boundary and anomaly-flagged cases), reported annually to the department chair or provost — not left to individual-instructor discretion (chain C6).
- Structure spot-checks as short, rubric-anchored, binary pass/fail ("authorship confirmed" / "not confirmed") rather than graded oral performance, to limit any coaching-access advantage (chain C5).
- Label transcript and course-grade components explicitly as individually-certified versus tool-assisted, rather than merging them into one opaque grade, so the credential stays legible to employers and accreditors (chain C2).
- Adopt one university-level AI-use disclosure tier system (e.g., Tier 0 — no AI; Tier 1 — AI-assisted, cited; Tier 2 — AI-primary, verified), published before each term starts, rather than leaving norms to individual-instructor discretion (chain C6).

**Falsifiable trigger conditions (when this recommendation flips):**
1. If an independently-audited AI-authorship-verification method reaches sub-1% false-positive and false-negative error, robust to hybrid human-AI text, and is deployed at production scale, shift weight toward unsupervised take-home (option B) and reduce reliance on in-room checkpoints (chain C2).
2. If a controlled study finds no significant outcome difference between hybrid-D graduates and pure-timed-exam graduates on licensure or professional outcomes, the hybrid's added complexity is not justified for non-licensure-bound programs, and a simpler architecture is preferable there (chain C6).
3. If the oral/process spot-check sampling floor cannot be funded, do not deploy an underfunded hybrid that manufactures false confidence — revert the certifying components to pure timed/in-person assessment (option A) instead (chain C6).
4. Wherever an external accreditation or licensure body mandates a specific proctored format for a given program, that mandate is a floor regardless of this analysis's general recommendation, independent of local pedagogical preference (chain C2).

The dominance result itself (C6's first hop, the trade-off's Pareto-dominance finding) is not the weak point — it was independently recomputed in the Adversarial pass and holds regardless of how the still-open GT-1/GT-13 questions resolve.
